title: Mental Models: Why a Latticework of Ideas Beats a Drawer Full of Facts
topic: tư duy: mạng lưới mô hình tư duy
unit: Mở đầu: học cách học & tấm bản đồ của một năm
summary: Charlie Munger argued that isolated facts are hard to use and that real understanding comes from a latticework of models drawn from many disciplines; chess research on chunking shows why organised knowledge works, and this year's twelve stages are a way to build that latticework.
body:
Most of us collect facts the way a drawer collects receipts: one at a time, each perfectly true, none connected to the others. Then a real problem arrives, at work or at home, and the drawer is no help. We know a lot, but we cannot *use* what we know.

In 1994, the investor Charlie Munger gave a talk at the University of Southern California's business school that has since become one of the most quoted speeches on how to think. Its central image is simple: knowledge should be built like a **latticework**, a criss-crossing frame of ideas from many fields, rather than a pile of isolated facts. This piece explains what he meant, why it works, and how to start building one this week.

## "Isolated facts" versus a latticework

Munger's point was blunt. In his words, "you can't really know anything if you just remember isolated facts and try and bang 'em back." And: "If the facts don't hang together on a latticework of theory, you don't have them in a usable form."

A **mental model** here means a compact idea about how some part of the world works: compound interest, supply and demand, feedback loops, incentives, the forgetting curve, confirmation bias. Each one is a lens. A fact tells you *what* happened; a model helps you see *why*, and predict what happens next.

The latticework is what you get when many such models, drawn from different disciplines, are connected to each other and to your own experience. Munger's advice was: "You've got to hang experience on a latticework of models in your head."

## Why one model is not enough: the man with a hammer

Munger's favourite warning came from an old saying: "To the man with only a hammer, every problem looks like a nail."

Someone trained only in law sees every problem as a question of rules. Someone trained only in accounting sees every problem as a number. Someone who only knows psychology sees motives everywhere. Each view is partly right, and each one alone produces confident, lopsided answers.

That is why Munger insisted that "the models have to come from multiple disciplines". He named mathematics, accounting, engineering and the hard sciences, biology, microeconomics, and what he called the psychology of misjudgment. He also offered a reassuring estimate: you don't need thousands of ideas. "80 or 90 important models will carry about 90% of the freight in making you a worldly-wise person."

## Why a latticework works: chunks and hooks

Two findings from cognitive science help explain why connected knowledge beats loose facts.

### Chunks: what chess masters really remember

In 1973, the psychologists William Chase and Herbert Simon tested how well chess players of different strengths could recall positions after a brief look at a board. With positions taken from real games, recall rose steadily with playing strength: masters reproduced boards that beginners could not. But with pieces scattered randomly, the masters' advantage largely disappeared (later research suggests they keep a small edge).

The explanation is **chunking**. A strong player doesn't see twenty-five separate pieces; they see a handful of familiar patterns, such as a castled king with its rook and surrounding pawns, and store each pattern as one unit. Their memory isn't bigger. Their knowledge is *organised*, so new information snaps onto existing structures. When the board makes no sense, the structure has nothing to grip.

A latticework of models is the everyday version of a chess master's library of patterns. When you understand incentives, a new regulation, a colleague's odd behaviour and a pricing trick at the market all become variations on a pattern you already hold.

### Hooks: new facts need somewhere to hang

Today's foundation article described the famous "washing clothes" experiment by Bransford and Johnson (1972): people who knew the topic of a vague passage *before* hearing it understood and remembered it far better. Knowledge you already have, once switched on, gives new information a place to land. The more connected your existing knowledge, the more hooks every new fact can catch on.

## Applying it to this week's theme: learning how to learn

This week, Studio is about learning itself, and the year's map you read today is, in effect, a plan for building a latticework.

Consider how the models from this week already connect:

- **The forgetting curve** (from yesterday) explains *when* to revisit ideas.
- **The generation effect** (from today's note-taking piece) explains *how* to revisit them: by producing answers, not rereading.
- **Advance organisers and schemas** explain why seeing the whole map *first* makes each stage easier.
- **Interleaving** explains why the year ends with four weeks of cross-stage review (*tổng ôn giao thoa*).
- **The Feynman technique** tests whether a model is really yours: can you explain it simply?

Five ideas, each useful alone, but together they form a small, sturdy frame: a theory of how Studio itself is built. That is a latticework in miniature.

Now look ahead. The twelve stages are deliberately drawn from different disciplines: family and housing, the state apparatus, customs and beliefs (*tín ngưỡng*), psychology, money, machines, the body, history, geopolitics, science, technology, and philosophy. That breadth is not decoration. It is Munger's "multiple disciplines" turned into a calendar.

## A worked example from working life

Imagine a common situation in a Vietnamese government office: a new administrative procedure (*thủ tục hành chính*) has been simplified on paper, yet people still queue at the commune-level one-stop counter (*bộ phận một cửa*), and complaints keep coming.

With one model, you get one answer. The legal lens says: the rules changed, so staff must apply them. Case closed.

With a latticework, you see more:

- **Incentives (economics):** Does any staff member gain or lose from the new process? Are performance targets measuring speed, or measuring the absence of errors?
- **Habit and status quo bias (psychology):** People keep doing what they did yesterday, even when a faster path exists.
- **Feedback loops (systems thinking):** If complaints go to a level that never talks to the counter staff, nothing corrects.
- **Bottlenecks (engineering):** A process is only as fast as its slowest step; maybe that is a single signature, not the counter.
- **Face and hierarchy (culture, *giữ thể diện*):** Junior staff may hesitate to report that the new form is confusing, so problems stay invisible.

None of these models is the "right" one. Together, they let you ask better questions, which is usually the most valuable thing a thoughtful person can bring to a meeting.

## How to build your latticework

You don't build a latticework by memorising a list of 80 models. You build it slowly, one solid model at a time, and by deliberately making connections.

1. **Name the model.** After each Studio article, ask: what is the one *idea about how things work* here, beyond the facts? Write it as a short rule, for example "people respond to what is measured, not to what is intended."
2. **Find a second home for it.** Ask where else the same model applies. If incentives explain the queue at the one-stop counter, where else do they show up: in the family, in traffic, in your own reading habits?
3. **Collide two models.** Once a week, take a situation and look at it through two models from different stages. Where do they agree? Where do they pull in opposite directions?
4. **Watch for your hammer.** Notice which lens you reach for first. If you always explain behaviour by personality, practise asking about incentives or systems instead.
5. **Keep it small and solid.** One model you truly understand, can explain simply and have used twice in real life is worth more than ten you've merely read about.

## A word of caution

The latticework idea is a heuristic, not a scientific theory, and it can be misused. Collecting models can become another way of collecting facts: a list of clever names with no real understanding behind them. Models also simplify; each leaves things out, and a confident model applied in the wrong place can mislead. The cure is the same as the method: test models against real situations, and keep more than one in view.

## In short

Isolated facts are hard to use; ideas that hang together on a frame of models become practical wisdom. Munger's latticework asks for models from many disciplines, so that you don't treat every problem as a nail. Chess research shows why: experts remember more because their knowledge is organised into patterns. This year's twelve stages are designed to give you those patterns, and your job is to connect them: name the model, find it a second home, and look at real problems through more than one lens.
